extra.message: Insecure Deserialization via pickle.loads on User-Controlled Data — Remote code execution on the server via crafted pickle payload [verified: pickle.loads() at line 75 receives attacker-controlled data from request.body or request.GET.get('blob') via acct_bundle_thaw_184; _wrk_gate() authentication exists at line 68 but pickle has no safe mode — arbitrary __reduce__ payloads execute on deserialization.]

Path Traversal — file write via ref parameter with sensitive data — Arbitrary file write; sensitive PII (SSN, credit card numbers) written to attacker-chosen filesystem paths. [verified: target = BASE_EXPORT_DIR / f'{ref}.json' at line 95 with unsanitized request.GET.get('ref'); path traversal sequences like '../../etc/cron' escape BASE_EXPORT_DIR and write JSON with SSN/card PII to attacker-chosen paths (with .json suffix).]

Server-Side Template Injection via Jinja2 Template Concatenation — Remote code execution via Jinja2 template expression injection [verified: Template('Result: ' + fragment).render() at line 145 concatenates user-controlled request.GET.get('fragment') into a Jinja2 template string and renders as HTML; Jinja2 expression syntax like {{config}} or {{''.__class__}} provides full Python object traversal and RCE.]

Server-Side Template Injection in Jinja2 rendering — Full server-side code execution; access to all Python objects, environment variables, and file system. [verified: Same as finding [2]: Template('Result: ' + fragment).render() at line 145 concatenates user GET param 'fragment' into Jinja2 template; SSTI enables Python object traversal and full RCE.]

OS Command Injection via acct_shell_probe_700 — Arbitrary shell command execution on the server with the application's privileges [verified: os.system('ping -c 1 ' + host) at line 161 concatenates unsanitized request.GET.get('host') directly into a shell command; shell metacharacters like ; | $() are not filtered, enabling arbitrary command execution.]

Command Injection via ping host parameter — Remote code execution with the privileges of the Django process — full server compromise. [verified: Same as finding [1]: os.system('ping -c 1 ' + host) at line 161 concatenates unsanitized request.GET.get('host') into a shell command with no sanitization; shell metacharacters enable arbitrary command execution.]

Path Traversal in Arbitrary File Write via acct_dock_shelf_719 — Arbitrary file write anywhere on the filesystem, potentially leading to RCE via cron/shell profile overwrite [verified: target = BASE_EXPORT_DIR / name at line 177 uses unsanitized request.GET.get('name') as a path component; '../' sequences allow writing request.body to arbitrary filesystem locations, enabling RCE via cron/SSH/profile overwrites.]

Hardcoded Default Django SECRET_KEY — Session forging, CSRF bypass, and cryptographic token compromise if deployed with default SECRET_KEY [verified: Line 11 sets SECRET_KEY to the well-known default 'django-insecure-local-dev-only-change-me' when the env var is absent; no compensating control exists — anyone knowing this string can forge Django sessions, CSRF tokens, and signed data.]

Hardcoded Django SECRET_KEY default — Session forgery, CSRF bypass, and cryptographic signature forgery if the default key is used in production. [verified: Same hardcoded SECRET_KEY default at line 11 as finding 0; no compensating control exists — the key is a publicly known insecure value that enables session and CSRF token forgery.]

Missing Rate Limiting on Authentication Endpoint — Unlimited brute-force password guessing against user accounts [verified: No rate-limiting, throttling, lockout, or CAPTCHA exists anywhere in the codebase — search for 'rate.limit|throttle|brute.force|AXES|django-axes|defender|captcha|login_attempt|lockout' across all Python files returned zero matches, and neither middleware nor settings configure any brute-force protection for the login endpoint.]

Sensitive Data (SSN/Credit Card) Written to Disk in Plaintext — Plaintext storage of SSNs and credit card numbers on the filesystem, exposed to anyone with server file access [verified: target.write_text(...) at line 97 writes SSN (request.GET.get('ssn')) and credit card (request.GET.get('card')) to a plaintext JSON file under BASE_EXPORT_DIR with no encryption; PII stored in cleartext on the filesystem.]

CORS Misconfiguration with Credentialed Origin Reflection — Credentialed cross-origin data theft from any malicious website targeting this endpoint [verified: acct_origin_mirror_660 at line 131-132 reflects request.headers.get('origin') directly into Access-Control-Allow-Origin and sets Access-Control-Allow-Credentials: 'true'; any origin can make credentialed cross-origin requests and read the JSON response.]

SSL Certificate Verification Disabled on Outbound Request — Man-in-the-middle attacks on server-to-server communications, enabling data interception and modification [verified: ssl._create_unverified_context() at line 189 creates an SSL context with certificate verification disabled; outbound HTTPS requests to partner.invalid are vulnerable to man-in-the-middle interception.]

DEBUG Mode Enabled by Default — Information disclosure via detailed error pages, exposed internal paths, and debug information [verified: Line 13 defaults DEBUG to True; with no env override, Django serves detailed error pages with stack traces, local variables, and settings — no middleware or configuration neutralizes this information disclosure path.]

Hardcoded Database Credentials in Default DATABASE_URL — If deployed without overriding DATABASE_URL, attackers with source access gain full database access [verified: Lines 56-60 hardcode 'postgres://crmuser:crmpass@localhost:5432/crm_db' as the DATABASES default; these credentials are committed in source and no runtime override or additional access control compensates for their exposure.]

Hardcoded Database Credentials in default DATABASE_URL — Database compromise if default credentials are used in production — full data access to all CRM records. [verified: Same hardcoded database credentials in the DATABASES default as finding 1; no runtime override or additional access guard compensates for their presence in source code.]

Unrestricted File Upload — no file type validation on documents — Stored XSS via uploaded HTML files served from /media/; potential for uploading executable files if deployment misconfigured. [verified: DocumentForm (crm/crm/forms.py:89) has a plain FileField with no FileExtensionValidator or content-type check, while OrganizationImportForm and ContactImportForm on the same file DO use FileExtensionValidator(['csv']) (lines 141,149), showing the control was deliberately omitted for documents. DEBUG defaults to True (core/settings.py:14) and core/urls.py:21-22 serves MEDIA_ROOT via static() in DEB]

IDOR: Missing organization access check in deal_create allows cross-tenant deal creation — An account manager can inject deals into any organization in the system, potentially polluting another tenant's pipeline, manipulating revenue data, or escalating privileges by creating deals they should not have access to. [verified: DealForm.Meta.fields includes 'organization' rendered as a plain Select with no queryset restriction, and deal_create only checks is_account_manager() without calling _org_access on the user-supplied organization FK; an account manager can POST any org ID and create a cross-tenant deal.]

IDOR: Missing Organization Access Check in escalation_create Allows Cross-Tenant Escalation Creation — Account managers can create escalations in organizations they do not manage, bypassing tenant isolation. Support agents can create escalations in any organization regardless of assignment. This enables data pollution, privilege escalation through assigned_agent self-assignment, and cross-tenant interference. [verified: escalation_create blocks only customer contacts but lets support agents and account managers through with no organization-scope check; form.save() commits the attacker-chosen organization field directly to the database, so an account manager for org A can create escalations in org B, and support agents can create escalations in any org and self-assign as assigned_agent.]

Authorization bypass: support agents can download documents from any organization without org-scope restriction — A support agent can exfiltrate internal documents (contracts, security questionnaires, invoices, internal notes) from any organization in the multi-tenant system, regardless of whether they have any legitimate relationship with that organization. This is a cross-tenant data breach. [verified: document_download for support agents only blocks VISIBILITY_BILLING docs but performs zero organization-scope check (no _org_access, no escalation-assignment verification); a support agent can download internal and customer-visible documents from any organization in the system.]

Cross-tenant access via unscoped organization lookup during contact import — An account manager can create customer contacts in any organization and then log in as those contacts to access another tenant's sensitive data including deals, escalations, documents, and internal notes. [verified: Same unscoped Organization.objects.filter(name=org_name) lookup in import_contacts as finding [4]; an account manager can create users with known passwords in any organization, enabling cross-tenant account takeover.]

Account enumeration via disabled-user check in login reveals account existence and correct password — An attacker performing credential stuffing can identify valid (username, password) pairs for disabled accounts, which may be re-enabled later or reused across services. The distinct error message confirms both existence and correct credentials. [verified: After AuthenticationForm.is_valid() succeeds (confirming both correct username and password), the code checks user.is_disabled and returns a distinct 'Your account has been disabled.' message, creating a reliable oracle that reveals both account existence and password correctness — distinct from the generic invalid-credentials error.]

Sensitive Data (Authorization Header) Written to Application Logs — Exposure of authentication tokens and sensitive request data in log files accessible to operators or stored in log aggregation systems [verified: logger.warning at line 42 logs raw request.body and request.headers.get('authorization') without redaction; tokens or credentials sent in these fields are written to application logs accessible via console handler.]

Open Redirect via Unvalidated lane Parameter — Phishing attacks and social engineering by redirecting users to attacker-controlled websites [verified: redirect(request.GET.get('lane', '/')) at line 51 passes unsanitized user input directly to Django's redirect(); no URL validation or allowlist check prevents redirecting to external phishing domains.]

Missing Authentication on Partner Console Endpoint — Unauthenticated access to an internal partner console endpoint, bypassing the x-internal-token security boundary [verified: acct_identity_ping_343 at line 106 has no _wrk_gate() call — confirmed by code inspection; every other partner console endpoint (17 others) gates with _wrk_gate, but this endpoint accepts and echoes user-supplied handle/channel without any authentication.]

Security Headers Intentionally Disabled — Browser XSS auditor and Content Security Policy protections are disabled, increasing XSS attack surface [verified: Response headers at lines 138-139 explicitly set X-XSS-Protection: '0' and Content-Security-Policy: ''; browser XSS auditor and CSP protections are disabled for this endpoint's responses, increasing XSS attack surface.]

Security Headers Disabled — XSS Protection and CSP Removed — Increased XSS attack surface — browser XSS auditor and CSP protections are disabled. [verified: Same as finding [14]: response headers at lines 138-139 set X-XSS-Protection: '0' and Content-Security-Policy: ''; browser XSS defenses intentionally disabled for this endpoint.]

Use of Insecure PRNG for Token Generation — If this code were used for security tokens, they could be predicted by an attacker observing previous outputs [verified: random.choice at line 172 uses Python's Mersenne Twister PRNG for code generation; if this code were used as a security token (reset token, API key), its output is predictable after observing enough values — the code is merely echoed, but the insecure primitive is present.]

Insecure Session and CSRF Cookie Flags When DEBUG is Enabled — Session and CSRF tokens transmitted over unencrypted HTTP, enabling session hijacking via network sniffing [verified: Lines 91-92 set SESSION_COOKIE_SECURE and CSRF_COOKIE_SECURE to 'not DEBUG'; when DEBUG defaults to True the Secure flag is absent and cookies transmit over unencrypted HTTP — no additional flag or HSTS preload compensates.]

Cross-Tenant Data Exposure: Support Agents See All Organizations in organization_list — Support agents gain unrestricted visibility into all organizations across all tenants, including organization names, billing contact emails, plans, statuses, and health scores. This violates tenant isolation and exposes sensitive business data beyond the agent's assigned scope. [verified: organization_list filters account managers by account_manager=request.user but support agents fall through to Organization.objects.all() with zero scope restriction; support agents can browse, search, and paginate all tenant organizations exposing names, billing contacts, plans, statuses, and health scores with no compensating middleware or decorator.]

Cross-tenant data exposure in document_list: support agents see documents from all orgs with any account manager — A support agent can enumerate and discover documents (names, categories, visibility levels, upload metadata) belonging to organizations they have no relationship with, violating multi-tenant isolation. This enables reconnaissance for targeted attacks on other tenants' document repositories. [verified: The support-agent document_list queryset uses Q(organization__account_manager__isnull=False) which matches all orgs with any account manager—not the requesting user—leaking document metadata across unrelated tenants.]

CSV Formula Injection in Data Exports — Code execution in spreadsheet applications when users open exported CSV files, enabling information exfiltration or malware execution [verified: User-controllable fields (org.name, org.billing_contact_name, org.internal_notes, esc.title) flow from OrganizationForm/EscalationForm into the DB and are written to CSV cells via csv.writer without any formula-character sanitization; no compensating validation or prefix stripping exists anywhere in the chain.]

CSV Formula Injection in Escalation Export — Attacker who can set escalation title, organization name, or username to a formula (e.g. =cmd|'/c calc'!A0) gains code execution on the machine of any user who opens the exported CSV in a spreadsheet application. [verified: export_escalations writes user-controlled esc.title, esc.organization.name, and esc.assigned_agent.username directly into CSV via csv.writer with no formula-escaping (e.g., prefixing ' to =/+/-/@); no sanitization utility exists in the codebase, so an attacker who can set an escalation title or org name to a formula payload gains code execution when a privileged user opens the CSV in Excel.]

CSV Formula Injection in Health Report Export — Attacker who can set organization name, internal notes, or account manager username to a spreadsheet formula gains arbitrary command execution on the machine of any platform admin who opens the exported health_report.csv. [verified: export_health_report writes org.name, org.internal_notes, and org.account_manager.username directly into CSV cells with no formula sanitization; an account manager or admin who sets org name/notes/username to a formula like =cmd|'/c calc'!A0 executes arbitrary commands when a platform admin opens health_report.csv in a spreadsheet.]

User enumeration and PII exposure to support agents via unfiltered global search — A support agent can search and enumerate all users in the system, exposing PII (full names, email addresses, usernames) beyond their authorized scope of assigned escalations. [verified: In global_search the support_agent branch sets organizations and deals to .none() but never filters the users queryset; support agents can enumerate all system users' full names and email addresses beyond their escalation scope.]

Information Disclosure via Exception Message with User Input — Leaks internal exception class names, user data in error context, and internal filesystem paths to attackers [verified: JsonResponse at line 37 returns str(exc) and exc.__class__.__name__ which includes user-supplied lot_ref and the BASE_EXPORT_DIR path; leaks internal filesystem structure and exception class names to aid reconnaissance.]

Information Disclosure via Exception Message in Response — Reconnaissance — attackers learn internal filesystem paths and application structure via error messages. [verified: Same as finding [11]: JsonResponse at line 37 returns str(exc) with user-supplied lot_ref embedded and exc.__class__.__name__, leaking BASE_EXPORT_DIR path and exception class names.]

Use of Cryptographically Weak MD5 Hash Algorithm — Hash collisions can be engineered; if this hash function were used for integrity verification, it would be bypassable [verified: hashlib.md5 at line 104 is used on user-supplied phrase with no security-sensitive downstream use visible; MD5 is cryptographically broken but the digest is only echoed back in JSON — no integrity verification is performed on it.]

Weak Cryptographic Hash — MD5 — Hash collisions; if MD5 output is used for integrity or identification, an attacker can craft inputs that produce the same hash. [verified: Same as finding [12]: hashlib.md5 at line 104 on user-supplied phrase; MD5 is cryptographically broken but the digest is only echoed back with no integrity verification dependency.]

Sensitive Configuration and Filesystem Path Leakage — Reveals Django settings module location and internal directory paths to aid attacker reconnaissance [verified: JsonResponse at line 198 exposes os.environ.get('DJANGO_SETTINGS_MODULE') and str(BASE_EXPORT_DIR); reveals internal server configuration paths useful for reconnaissance but requires the ops token to access.]

Environment Variable and Path Disclosure in Response — Reconnaissance — attackers learn the Django settings module path and internal file export directory. [verified: Same as finding [10]: JsonResponse at line 198 exposes DJANGO_SETTINGS_MODULE env var and BASE_EXPORT_DIR path; internal configuration details leaked for reconnaissance.]

Raw API Key Material Stored in Session via Django Messages — API key exposure — raw key material accessible in session storage; potential for key theft if sessions are compromised or persisted insecurely. [verified: Raw API key material is passed via messages.success() which, with no MESSAGE_STORAGE override, stores it in the default session-backed message storage; the secret persists server-side until consumed.]

Raw API Key Material Stored in Session via Django Messages on Key Rotation — Raw API key material is stored in plaintext in the session backend. An attacker who compromises the session store, gains access to session data, or exploits session fixation can recover the full API key and use it to authenticate as the organization. [verified: apikey_rotate stores the full raw API key in Django messages.success() which defaults to session storage; the raw key persists in plaintext in the session backend until the next page load consumes the message, though the exposure window is typically brief and the key is already displayed to the authenticated user in the HTTP response.]
